## Why This Is Asked
Probe ability to build a scalable, dynamic interval tracker with precise deletions and constrained queries on large domains.

## Key Concepts
- Dynamic segment tree with range-add and range-max
- Lazy propagation for O(log U) updates
- ID-based removal and duplicate handling
- Memory proportional to active intervals × log U

## Code Example
```javascript
class Node{constructor(){this.max=0;this.add=0;this.l=null;this.r=null}}
function add(n,lo,hi,L,R,v){if(!n) n=new Node(); if(L<=lo&&hi<=R){n.max+=v; n.add+=v; return n} let mid=(lo+hi)>>1; if(L<=mid){n.l=add(n.l,lo,mid,L,R,v)} if(R>mid){n.r=add(n.r,mid+1,hi,L,R,v)} n.max=Math.max(n.l?.max||0, n.r?.max||0) + (n.add||0); return n}
function query(n,lo,hi,L,R){if(!n) return 0; if(L<=lo&&hi<=R) return n.max; const mid=(lo+hi)>>1; let res= n.add||0; if(L<=mid) res=Math.max(res, (n.l?query(n.l,lo,mid,L,R):0)); if(R>mid) res=Math.max(res, (n.r?query(n.r,mid+1,hi,L,R):0)); return res}
```

- How would you modify to support maxOverlapInRange with dynamic coordinate compression? 
- How would you adapt for memory reuse when many intervals expire simultaneously?

questions.explanation:
## Why This Is Asked
Dynamic range order-statistics in a mutable sequence is a practical problem appearing in text editors, collaborative applications, and database engines. It tests the ability to combine balanced binary search trees with order-statistics structures and manage update propagation carefully.

## Key Concepts
- Implicit data structures (position-based, not key-based)
- Range k-th statistics with duplicates
- Augmented BSTs (treap, red-black tree)
- Multiset or Fenwick tree per subtree node
- Coordinate compression for value domains

## Approach
An implicit treap stores the sequence by position, with each node augmented to contain a data structure representing all values in its subtree. When performing insertAt(i, v) or eraseAt(i), standard treap splits and merges propagate updates through O(log n) nodes, each updating its auxiliary structure in O(log n)—resulting in O(log² n) amortized time.

For rangeKth(l, r, k), split the treap into three segments, extract the middle [l, r] portion, and query the k-th smallest using the aggregated multisets or BIT at the root of that segment. After obtaining the answer, merge the three parts back together.

## Alternatives
A segment tree of multisets (or BITs over compressed values) provides similar complexity but with different trade-offs: more memory overhead for the explicit tree structure, but potentially simpler implementation and better cache locality.

## Complexity Summary
| Operation | Time | Space |
|-----------|------|-------|
| insertAt | O(log² n) | O(log n) per update |
| eraseAt | O(log² n) | O(log n) per update |
| rangeKth | O(log² n) | O(1) |

## Trade-offs
- **Implicit Treap**: Handles dynamic sequences naturally; splits/merges are built-in; slightly more complex augmentation logic
- **Segment Tree of BITs**: Better for static value domains; simpler overall structure; higher memory usage for dense trees

## Why This Is Asked
Tests mastering of dynamic trees for weighted path queries, a practical need in graph-based workloads with frequent updates.

## Key Concepts
- Link-Cut Tree (LCT) with edge-nodes representation
- Path queries via expose/access and splay aggregations
- Maintaining order statistics across edge-nodes on a path for kthLargest

## Code Example
```javascript

class EdgeNode { constructor(weight, id) { this.weight = weight; this.sum = weight; /* plus pointers */ } }
```

questions.explanation: The problem asks for an interval-based weight data structure with dynamic insertion and deletion by id, plus point queries that aggregate all covering intervals. The segment-tree-on-compressed-coordinates approach cleanly localizes interval coverage into O(log N) nodes per update, enabling efficient sums and kth-weight queries. Per-node multisets (or PBDS trees) provide fast counts and order statistics, enabling precise kth-largest computations across overlapping intervals. Key trade-offs: memory vs. query speed; use coordinate compression to bound tree size.
